comments.text: When people discuss quality, they usually neglect to delineate what the quality is referring to. Most often, it’s material and craftsmanship. But something I think is worth highlighting is the quality of OWNERSHIP. Is it easy to wash or repair? Does it wear and age nicely? I think these ideas are also congruent to the conversation of quality, because ultimately, we want a higher quality of LIVING, not just a more technologically advanced form of plastic (Gore-Tex, DryVent, etc.) that is shaped to our bodies.
This was a missed opportunity to discuss Bronson and quality compared to japanese and heritage brands, and the nature of quality and value

My wife was a designer for a major fashion brand that everyone knows. The design offices are in NYC. When they used to source fabric from China, some of the factories would offer design services for basic stuff. Because her company's design team was so huge, they never used it. But if they had, no one would ever know the difference. Menswear design changes are tiny compared to women, and what Bronson is doing is a smart evolutionary response to the tariffs that have forced U.S. companies to move production to other countries.

One of the things my wife says is that the technical knowledge of Chinese factories are second to none, and for some things, only Chinese factories can do it for a reasonable price. A lot of them have moved operations to Italy and Vietnam.

Nice explanation.  Same thing is happening in the camera / cinema lens market.  The Chinese “brands” are producing some top notch modern and classic looking lenses at way lower prices.  And since those lenses were originally patented, lots of the information needed to make them is in the public domain.

Anyways, mama sewed polo shirts at one time.... and at the end of the line, they would sort them by quality tier and order fulfillment. Of the Chinese "selvedge-style" brands (I use that as a loose catch-all), my experience has been that Sauce Zhan is consistently the highest in quality, with Bronson coming a pretty close second. After that you get Red Tornado, Bob Dong and a couple of others, but they are not, IMO, as good. 
I used to work at Rivet and Hide in London, and have a good number of jeans, shirts and jackets from, eg, PBJ, IH, UES, Stevenson and Rogue Territory etc. To me, PBJ are still the gold standard in denim, but Sauce Zhan is really not far behind, especially if you check out their boutique line, "Sauce Origin" (though some of the prices of that sub-brand are approaching Japanese levels).
Bronson are more explicitly biased towards re-workings of specific items of apparel from the glory days of US workwear and military stuff, and I like their stuff very much if that's what I want to recreate. Their customer service is unusually good, and if they have any doubts or questions on sizing they are in touch immediately to recommend and make sure you are aware of any issues. I hover between L and XL in most Chinese stuff (5'11 and 78kg); the last batch I bought I ordered all L, and they contacted me within about 6 hours to say that they thought XL was a better fit in this particular case, and they were right. Also, their shipping is fast and efficient, for me usually about 7-10 days to Europe, and occasionally as little as 5 days. Never any issues with Customs.

I picked up on something small in your presentation, but which I felt might be worth digging into. That sweater at 3:50. I’m not fond of acrylic fiber myself, especially the environmental impact of new synthetic production, but acrylic doesn’t necessarily increase pilling likelihood when blended with wool. The fiber preparation and structure matter much more - that construction you showed is likely worsted-spun for durability and would actually be quite pill-resistant despite the 20% acrylic content, though it’s honestly difficult to determine the spinning method with certainty from the video.

The worsted preparation keeps fibers aligned and reduces surface exposure, while coarse wool fibers are naturally too stiff to tangle easily. Most commercial sweaters that pill heavily use fine fibers in woolen preparations, creating far more exposed fiber ends than a small percentage of acrylic would contribute.

That 1x1 ribbing also creates a denser fabric structure that helps prevent pill formation. While there are certainly exposed fibers in any machine knit, this particular combination - coarse, likely worsted-spun, ribbed construction - would probably outperform typical fine-fiber woolens in pilling resistance, regardless of the synthetic blend percentage.

Two thoughts on the pricing:

1. A lot of Chinese D2C brands are cheaper because they are not paying import duties (now commonly called tariffs). The tax code specifically different duty rates for different products and different origins, you'd be surprised how high they can be. It's usually double digit percentages. For brands operating in the US the brand is the importer, so the import duty is baked into the retail price. For D2C brands you are the importer so you might get slapped with a big tariff bill on delivery.

2. The design process is expensive. As a brand you have to do research, pay patterners to draw patterns, grade it for multiple sizes, then order expensive samples multiple times for corrections. Then some other factory comes along, takes your piece, copies the pattern, and sells it under their own white label for much cheaper. Clothing patterns are not copyrightable so good luck getting recourse. This is less of an issue with work wear brands where everyone is using the same original 501 or OG107 design though.

Anyways I've done a lot of yapping on pricing and morals, TLDR it's complicated and there's no clean solution, as irritating as it may be.
